n: A prayer for God's mercy and kindness is a type of lament. Sometimes, the psalmist asks for mercy because he recognizes his own weakness and sin (see also {{Psalm 6:2|Psalm 6:2}}; {{Psalm 9:13|9:13}}; {{Psalm 25:16|25:16}}; {{Psalm 31:9|31:9}}; {{Psalm 41:4|41:4}}, {{Psalm 41:10|10}}). Other times, the plea comes from the psalmist's dedication to the Lord (see {{Psalm 26:11|Psalm 26:11}}; {{Psalm 27:7|27:7}}; {{Psalm 119:29|119:29}}, {{Psalm 119:58|58}}, {{Psalm 119:132|132}}). In every situation, God's mercy leads to inner renewal.
The person who regrets their wrongdoing cannot offer anything to God. They need God's favor, mercy, forgiveness, and blessing to experience renewal and restoration.

Psalm 51 is a poem about admitting sin. David’s sins against Bathsheba and Uriah show how serious and hurtful sin is.

Sins committed against other people are also committed against God. This is because God made everyone and he has tender and faithful love for them. The Israelites understood that sin made them unclean. It kept them from being in God’s presence. This was like being sent away from God and having the Holy Spirit taken from them.

God provided several ways for the Israelites to be made clean and pure. One way was to dip a hyssop plant into special water. Then the water would be sprinkled on someone to wash them (Numbers 19). Another way was to make sin offerings or burnt offerings.

Being washed and making sacrifices were important parts of how the Israelites worshipped God. But they only showed what happened on the outside of a person’s body. They didn’t show what happened inside the person’s heart. In their heart is where people can feel truly sorry for their sin.

God cares deeply about people’s hearts. When people sin, they must make themselves humble before God. They must be completely honest and recognise all that they have done wrong. This is what it means to have a broken spirit. The spirit is the spiritual part of a person. People offer their broken spirit to God. They ask him to have mercy and to forgive them.

Only God can take away a person’s guilt. He can make a person able to say no to sin. He can make people able to be faithful to him.

This heartfelt prayer for restoration seeks God's favor, mercy, forgiveness, and cleansing. With a broken spirit, the psalmist admits his sin and takes responsibility ({{Psalm 51:3-6|Psalm 51:3–6}}). He then asks God to remove his guilt and renew him internally ({{Psalm 51:7-12|Psalm 51:7–12}}). The psalmist commits again to living wisely and joyfully while serving God and others ({{Psalm 51:13-17|Psalm 51:13–17}}).
See {{2 Samuel 11:1-27|2 Samuel 11:1–27}}. The psalm does not directly mention this event.

These psalms of David share a common theme. They reflect on the experience of evil. In {{Psalm 51:1-19|Psalm 51}}, the psalmist admits his wrongdoing and asks for God's forgiveness. {{Psalm 52:1-64:10|Psalms 52–64}} express sorrow over specific evils David faced. A song of praise ({{Psalm 65:1-13|Psalm 65}}) brings David's laments to an end.

*Wash me … cleanse me*: The psalmist asks for cleansing and freedom from the guilt of his sin ({{Psalm 51:7|Psalm 51:7}}; see {{Psalm 26:6|26:6}}; {{Isaiah 1:16|Isaiah 1:16}}, {{Isaiah 1:18|18}}; {{Isaiah 4:4|4:4}}).
The psalmist accepts the results of his sin against God. He understands that he has no goodness without God's renewal.

*Against You, You only*: This is an exaggeration. The psalmist knows he also sinned against people ({{2 Samuel 11:2-4|2 Samuel 11:2–4}}, {{2 Samuel 11:15-17|15–17}}), but his sin against God is more important. He expects God to rebuke him and will accept whatever verdict God gives (see {{Romans 3:4|Romans 3:4}}).
*I was brought forth in iniquity*: The psalmist is not making excuses but is admitting how deep his sinfulness is. From the time we are conceived, we all share in the human condition of sinfulness.

*Purify me with hyssop* (literally *Purify me with the hyssop branch*; see {{Exodus 12:22|Exodus 12:22}}; {{Leviticus 14:4|Leviticus 14:4}}; {{John 19:29|John 19:29}}; {{Hebrews 9:19|Hebrews 9:19}}): The psalmist relies on God to cleanse and renew him (see {{Isaiah 1:18|Isaiah 1:18}}).

- Regaining joy is a gracious gift from God. 

- *You have crushed*: The psalmist feels completely broken ({{Psalm 6:2|Psalm 6:2}}; compare {{Psalm 34:20|34:20}}).
A loyal spirit produces inner strength. It helps a person remain faithful and continue even during difficulty.
God’s Spirit renews and recreates the human spirit.
*Your Holy Spirit*: Only the Holy Spirit can change a person's will to make it "right" ({{Psalm 51:10|Psalm 51:10}}) and "willing" to obey ({{Psalm 51:12|51:12}}).
As he learns from his sin and its consequences, the psalmist wants to teach others.

*bloodguilt*: This expression refers to any injustice, not only killing someone ({{Psalm 9:12|Psalm 9:12}}; {{Psalm 58:10|58:10}}; see {{2 Samuel 11:14-26|2 Samuel 11:14–26}}; compare {{Isaiah 1:15-17|Isaiah 1:15–17}}).

*build up the walls of Jerusalem*: These verses were likely added as a prayer for national restoration after the exile (see {{Psalm 42:1-43:5|Psalms 42–43}}). The entire community in exile shared the feelings expressed in this psalm.

Sacrifices made with the right intentions come from a heart that is right with God and others (see {{Psalm 15:2-5|Psalms 15:2–5}}; {{Psalm 24:3-6|24:3–6}}; {{Psalm 50:14|50:14}}; {{Matthew 5:23-24|Matthew 5:23–24}}).
The accuser, Doeg the Edomite, is an example of a person who chose to do evil.

Liars deceive themselves by thinking they can be heroes with their words. They see themselves as innocent, even though they love evil and cause harm. Those who speak curses, sarcasm, bitterness, arrogant boasting, and lies ({{Psalm 31:18|Psalms 31:18}}; {{Psalm 34:13|34:13}}; {{Psalm 59:7|59:7}}, {{Psalm 59:12|12}}; {{Psalm 120:2-3|120:2–3}}; {{Psalm 140:3|140:3}}, {{Psalm 140:9|9}}) create chaos, isolation, and destruction ({{James 3:5|James 3:5}}). Their sharp words cut like swords and daggers ({{Psalm 55:21|Psalms 55:21}}; {{Psalm 57:4|57:4}}; {{Psalm 64:3|64:3}}), the fangs of a snake ({{Psalm 140:3|140:3}}), or a razor.

Wicked people use words to destroy relationships and communities. They foolishly think that they can be heroes by their words ({{Psalm 52:1-4|Psalm 52:1–4}}), but their downfall comes suddenly ({{Psalm 52:5-7|52:5–7}}). In contrast, the godly renew their commitment to the Lord ({{Psalm 52:8-9|Psalm 52:8–9}}) and find security in their future with him.
Dishonest speech can change a person's character.
God will strike the wicked down like a pagan altar, idol, or unclean vessel ({{Exodus 34:13|Exodus 34:13}}; {{Leviticus 11:35|Leviticus 11:35}}; {{2 Kings 10:27|2 Kings 10:27}}).
God’s judgment on the wicked will come suddenly and forcibly. The godly rejoice in God’s justice, not in the misfortunes of the wicked.
*see and fear*: In Hebrew, these words sound almost alike.

- The psalmist commits himself to a life of trust in the Lord.

- An olive tree can live a long time with proper care ({{Psalm 1:3|Psalms 1:3}}; {{Psalm 128:3|128:3}}). The psalmist wants to be near the Lord, who is his Savior and the source of his blessings ({{Psalm 18:6|Psalms 18:6}}; {{Psalm 23:6|23:6}}).
Paul uses the Greek translation of this passage to describe the moral corruption of all people ({{Romans 3:10-12|Romans 3:10–12}}).
This psalm is similar to {{Psalm 14:1-7|Psalm 14}}, with differences only in verse 5.

*scattered the bones*: Israel's enemies would face a shameful defeat and would not have the peaceful rest of a proper burial (compare {{Psalm 141:7|Psalm 141:7}}; {{2 Kings 9:10|2 Kings 9:10}}; {{Jeremiah 8:1-2|Jeremiah 8:1–2}}; {{Ezekiel 6:5|Ezekiel 6:5}}).
The Ziphites intended to use violence.

This personal lament was caused by violent and godless people ({{Psalm 54:3|Psalm 54:3}}). The psalmist prays to God and focuses on God's help ({{Psalm 54:4|54:4}}). He asks God to save him from evil and judge his enemies ({{Psalm 54:5|Psalm 54:5}}, {{Psalm 54:7|7}}).

- The strangers were excluded from the covenant community (see {{Psalm 109:11|Psalm 109:11}}; {{Proverbs 5:10|Proverbs 5:10}}). 

- Proud and violent people do not respect God or others (see {{Psalm 35:11|Psalms 35:11}}, {{Psalm 35:25|25}}; {{Psalm 86:14|86:14}}; {{Proverbs 11:16|Proverbs 11:16}}).
A voluntary offering is a sacrifice of praise. Sacrifices of praise are the kind of offering God most desires (see {{Psalm 50:14-15|Psalm 50:14–15}}, {{Psalm 50:23|23}}).
In anticipation of God’s response, the mood of the psalm changes from sorrow to thanksgiving.
The occasion for this prayer is an attack by an enemy.

The psalmist faces enemies led by a former friend ({{Psalm 55:12-14|Psalm 55:12–14}}). This causes him great distress. He prays to the Lord and trusts him for justice ({{Psalm 55:22-23|Psalm 55:22–23}}). 

Jesus went through similar pain when Judas, his friend, betrayed him. He also experienced the psalmist’s prayer being answered: 

- by taking the place of the wicked and receiving their punishment ({{Isaiah 53:7-9|Isaiah 53:7–9}}), and

- by trusting the Father, who saved ({{Luke 23:46|Luke 23:46}}) and rewarded him ({{Isaiah 53:10-12|Isaiah 53:10–12}}).
In the experience of deep anguish, the psalmist confesses that his adversity has become unbearable and he seeks an escape.
The psalmist's enemy used to be a friend. Remembering their close relationship causes him pain (see {{Psalm 31:11|Psalm 31:11}}).
God is good and faithful, but the psalmist’s enemies and so-called friend are deceitful and wicked.
The psalmist commits all his cares to the Lord.
To die young means missing out on God's full blessings (compare {{Proverbs 3:2|Proverbs 3:2}}, {{Proverbs 3:16|16}}).

- *A Miktam*: This may be a literary or musical term.

- David was *seized* by *Philistines* concerned about his loyalties and brought before King Achish ({{1 Samuel 21:10-15|1 Samuel 21:10–15}}).
In this lament, the psalmist first asks for help and then expresses confidence in God. This pattern occurs two times ({{Psalm 56:1-4|Psalm 56:1–4}}, {{Psalm 56:5-13|5–13}}).
*man*: Or *mere flesh,* in contrast to God, who is immortal and much more powerful (see {{Isaiah 2:22|Isaiah 2:22}}).
The psalmist specifies his charge against his attackers as he prays for their evil to end.
The psalmist uses wordplay with two similar Hebrew words: *wanderings* (*nod*) and *bottle* (*no’d*).

*man* (Hebrew *’adam*): The psalm also uses two other words for man: 

- *’enosh* (meaning “people,” {{Psalm 56:1|Psalm 56:1}}) and

- *basar* (meaning “mere mortals,” {{Psalm 56:4|Psalm 56:4}}).

All these words point to the short and limited nature of human life.
The light of God’s goodness and salvation will replace the darkness of death (see {{Psalm 18:25-29|Psalms 18:25–29}}; {{Psalm 27:1|27:1}}).
*shadow of Your wings*: Like a bird protects its young, God protects those who trust in him (see {{Psalm 17:8|Psalm 17:8}}).

The psalmist asks for mercy and protection, then expresses trust and confidence in the Lord ({{Psalm 57:1-4|Psalm 57:1–4}}). When the wicked fall into their own traps ({{Psalm 57:6|Psalm 57:6}}), the psalmist will praise the Lord ({{Psalm 57:7-10|57:7–10}}).

- *God Most High* (Hebrew *Elohim-Elyon*) is a common title for God. He is more powerful than all real or imagined supernatural beings (see {{Psalm 91:1|Psalms 91:1}}; {{Psalm 97:9|97:9}}; {{Genesis 14:18-22|Genesis 14:18–22}}). 

- *who fulfills His purpose for me*: Or *who will end my [trouble]*, or *who deals kindly with me*.

These verses are a prayer for rescue from strong enemies. The metaphor of fierce lions describes human foes. The psalmist feels unable to escape them without God's help (see also {{Psalm 35:11-21|Psalms 35:11–21}}; {{Psalm 124:6|124:6}}).

- This verse appears again in {{Psalm 57:11|Psalm 57:11}} and {{Psalm 108:5|108:5}}. 

- God's glory, which is his visible presence that keeps out all evil ({{Psalm 8:1|Psalm 8:1}}; {{Psalm 19:1-4|19:1–4}}; {{Psalm 24:7|24:7}}), will fill the entire creation ({{Isaiah 6:3|Isaiah 6:3}}).
The psalmist is sure that God will stop the night of evil (compare {{Psalm 56:13|Psalm 56:13}}).
This section is repeated with a few changes in {{Psalm 108:1-5|Psalm 108:1–5}}.
God's glory reaches the entire universe, and people will praise his constant love and faithfulness.

*rulers* (or *gods*): People used this term for high officials and administrators of justice ({{Psalm 82:1|Psalm 82:1}}, {{Psalm 82:6|6}}). In other contexts, it might refer to angelic creatures ({{Psalm 89:7|Psalm 89:7}}) or the gods of other nations ({{Psalm 82:1|82:1}}; {{Daniel 11:36|Daniel 11:36}}).
The administrators of justice were furthering their own interests rather than those of the needy. The absence of justice gradually resulted in a violent society.

The administration of justice is a mark of good government. God expects nothing less from his people. The psalmist condemns Israel’s leaders for abusing their power, and he calls on the Lord to rain down his curses upon the wicked. The demonstration of divine justice will reassure the godly that God is just.

All humans are born with a tendency to sin (see {{Psalm 51:5|Psalm 51:5}}). However, the wicked follow their sinful desires, while the godly struggle against them ({{Romans 7:19-23|Romans 7:19–23}}; {{James 4:1-10|James 4:1–10}}).
The psalmist calls on God to break the destructive power of the wicked.
When moving over dry ground, slugs dry up.
God’s judgment will come suddenly. The certainty of vindication brings joy to the godly.
Being shown to be right is the reward for those who live for God.
*protect me* (or *lift me up high*): When surrounded by evil, the godly pray for God to set them apart for himself and protect them.
The psalmist laments the power of enemies who conspire with other nations.
The psalmist asks God not to show mercy to the treacherous, deceptive, and wicked traitors (see {{Psalm 25:2|Psalm 25:2}}).
The wicked threaten like aggressive dogs, but the Lord shows that he does not fear them.
The psalmist prays that the wicked will suffer the same pain they have caused others.
The wicked will remain unsatisfied, but the psalmist will praise the Lord's strength and loving devotion.

- This psalm was taught to young people as part of their education. 

- *When*: See {{2 Samuel 8:13-14|2 Samuel 8:13–14}}. 

- *Aram-naharaim* and *Aram-zobah* refer to the Arameans of northwest Mesopotamia and Syria (see study note on Genesis 24:10). 

- The tune *“Lily of the Testimony”* is unknown today.
When God’s people experience his discipline, they affirm their loyalty and await God’s answer.
The psalmist laments a national defeat and cries out to God for rescue.

*we are staggered from the wine: Yayin*, the Hebrew word for "wine," is often associated with drunkenness ({{2 Samuel 13:28|2 Samuel 13:28}}; {{Isaiah 5:11|Isaiah 5:11}}; {{Isaiah 28:7-8|28:7–8}}; see also {{Psalm 104:15|Psalm 104:15}}; {{Deuteronomy 14:26|Deuteronomy 14:26}}; {{Isaiah 55:1|Isaiah 55:1}}). It symbolized God's judgment on the wicked ({{Psalm 75:8|Psalm 75:8}}; {{Jeremiah 51:7|Jeremiah 51:7}}).

- God raised a banner over his people to serve as a rallying point and as a source of pride and confidence. 

- The fear of God that leads to wisdom ({{Psalm 111:10|Psalm 111:10}}) is not weakness. It gives the perspective and strength needed to do what is right.
The psalmist prays for rescue based on the special relationship between God and his people.

Shechem and Succoth represent the heartland of Israel.

These places were located in the central region of the land. Because of this, they can represent the center of Israel’s life and strength.
The Lord responds with a message of promise. He shares his land with his people as spoils of war.
Destroying the capital (*the fortified city*) of a defeated invader would help prevent future attacks. Edom's capital was Bozrah, located to the southeast of Israel. Only God could grant victory.
